_comment: REAL CASE LIBRARY -- 13 of the 18 structured RCA cases from docs/Boiler_Failure_Case_Studies_RCA.pdf (AFBC captive boiler, the correct asset class). Five cases are held out in data/kb/holdout.json and are ABSENT here, not down-weighted. Each case_id RCA-NN == 'Case N' in the PDF. `pdf_case`/`source` carry provenance; `family` is the PDF's six-family classification and is used only by the coverage/discriminability analysis, not by the matcher. Signatures are expressed in our (tag, direction, band) vocabulary over the six tags plus the water_balance / energy_balance pseudo-tags L1 emits; every real signal that is NOT one of the six tags is written into discriminating_evidence as a go-observe instruction, never invented as a tag. PROVISIONAL: hold-out split and the episode->case_id re-pointing (reports/stage5_case_library.md) both await advisor ratification.

cases.title: Drum level low leading to water-wall starvation - feed control valve actuator seizure
cases._signature_note: Corrected Stage 5 review: Case 1 describes feed flow STUCK BELOW steam ('feed flow reads 4-5 TPH less than steam flow', 'no further increase in feed flow'), not feed flow falling. So feed_water_flow is FLAT, and the discriminator is the sustained negative feed-minus-steam mismatch, carried by the water_balance DEFICIT triple (opposite sign to RCA-11's SURPLUS - this is the Case 1 vs Case 11 pair the balance layer exists to separate).
hypotheses: H1 feed-side hydraulic deficiency - BFP degradation or suction problem
H2 feed path restriction / control failure - FCV stuck, strainer choked, MOV throttled
H3 uncontrolled water loss - CBD/EBD/low-point drain inadvertently open
H4 water wall or economiser tube leak dumping water into the furnace
H5 false level indication - condensate pot leak or transmitter drift
H6 sudden load swing causing shrink and a transient level dip
cases.discriminating_evidence: Feed control valve demand saturated at 100% with feed flow not responding. This separates a control/actuation failure from every other cause: a pump problem shows low BFP discharge pressure with the valve still modulating; a tube leak shows furnace hissing plus boiler-water conductivity FALLING; a false instrument shows no real flow imbalance. Go observe (not in the six tags): FCV position feedback vs demand at the panel; BFP discharge header pressure and motor current against the head-flow curve; boiler-water conductivity trend (here RISING/concentrating, which also argues against a large blow-down loss); furnace listening check for a steam leak; agreement of the two level transmitters and the gauge glass; standby BFP auto-start on demand (a latent failure).
cases.root_cause: Feed water control valve actuator stem seizure from deposit build-up and lack of exercise; aggravated by an inadvertently part-open continuous blow-down valve and a latent standby-BFP auto-start failure. Systemic: no PM regime for periodic FCV stroking/calibration, no proof-test of the standby BFP auto-start, no field valve line-up verification.

cases.title: Main steam temperature high - heat-input to steam-flow imbalance after HP heater loss
hypotheses: H1 loss of HP heater -> low feed water temperature -> increased firing and superheat
H2 inadequate spray / attemperator capacity or a failed spray control valve
H3 excess air shifting heat pick-up towards the convective superheater
H4 soot on the water walls reducing evaporator absorption, raising gas temperature into the SH
H5 delayed combustion / over-feeding the upper compartments carrying the flame front up
H6 faulty steam temperature indication
cases.discriminating_evidence: Measured spray flow rising in step with a 100% spray-valve opening while steam temperature still climbs. That proves the attemperator hardware is healthy and the disturbance is an increased heat-release-to-steam-flow ratio, not a control-element failure. Go observe (not in the six tags): economiser inlet feed water temperature (here down ~30 degC after HP heater isolation); spray control valve position AND spray flow measurement together; O2 at economiser outlet (here in the normal 3-4% band, weakening the excess-air hypothesis); SH tube metal temperatures against a defined action limit; furnace-exit / post-SH flue gas temperature; compartment-wise feeder trends (uniform here, not top-heavy); coal CV vs the feeder calibration basis.
cases.root_cause: Loss of the HP heater and the resulting low economiser inlet feed water temperature, compensated by increased firing at constant load, exceeding the design single-stage attemperation capacity. Systemic: no operating rule linking HP heater unavailability to a mandatory load reduction and revised temperature-control strategy, plus an HP heater maintenance backlog.

cases.title: Main steam temperature low with water hammer - passing attemperator spray control valve
hypotheses: H1 sharp load increase with lagging firing rate and low air flow (combustion deficit)
H2 passing / stuck attemperator spray valve or leaking by-pass, over-spraying the steam
H3 high drum level causing moisture carry-over into the superheater
H4 faulty drum separators allowing carry-over even at normal level
H5 too high feed water temperature / excessive economiser absorption
H6 faulty steam temperature indication
cases.discriminating_evidence: Spray flow registered while spray demand is zero and the controller output is closed - a passing spray control valve, which no other hypothesis explains. Go observe (not in the six tags): attemperator spray flow vs spray demand and valve position; audible knocking / hammering in the main steam line near the stop valve; turbine differential expansion trend (here negative); saturated- and main-steam sample conductivity (here rising = moisture carry-over); combustion air flow and O2 for the new firing rate (here air on the low end, O2 below 2%); SH tube metal temperature falling with steam temperature.
cases.root_cause: Seat leakage of the attemperator spray control valve (passing in the closed position), unmasked by a sharp turbine load increase in which firing rate and air flow lagged and the drum swelled. Systemic: no periodic passing / seat-tightness test for the spray valve, no boiler-friendly TG load ramp-rate limit, and a defect-reporting culture that left a known passing valve unlogged.

cases.title: Main steam pressure high on load rejection - pressure relief path fail-to-open
hypotheses: H1 sudden load rejection with fuel input not reduced quickly enough
H2 failure of the pressure relief path (PRDS dumping control valve) to open on demand
H3 uncontrolled fuel entry - coal feeder speed control fault / feeders not cutting back
H4 pressure control loop failure or wrong set point
H5 faulty pressure indication causing an unnecessary intervention
H6 safety valves set too high / not lifting at the correct pressure
cases.discriminating_evidence: PRDS dumping control valve demand present in DCS with no corresponding valve-position feedback movement. The load rejection alone would have been absorbed within the safety-valve margin had the dumping path opened. Go observe (not in the six tags): TG trip / reverse-power signal and ESV closure (the initiating event); PRDS dumping valve demand vs position feedback; coal feeder speed vs the cutback command (here a ~70 s lag before feeders responded); safety valve lift at the stamped set pressures (72 / 74 kg/cm2(g)); agreement of the three independent pressure transmitters and the local gauge.
cases.root_cause: Fail-to-open of the PRDS dumping control valve on demand, so the designed pressure-relief route was unavailable during a foreseeable turbine trip, compounded by a delayed manual fuel cutback against the thermal inertia of the fluidised bed. Systemic: no periodic in-service proof test of the dumping valve, and no automatic fuel-runback / bed-slumping interlock on turbine trip.

cases.title: Bed temperature high leading to clinker formation - loss of ash recirculation cooling
hypotheses: H1 high CV / low ash coal raising heat release per unit of bed material
H2 low PA / SA flow reducing convective heat removal from the bed and fluidisation quality
H3 sudden load change causing a fuel-air mismatch
H4 faulty bed temperature thermocouple giving a spurious high reading
H5 ash recirculation system trouble - cool ash not being returned to the bed
H6 faulty bed ash draining letting bed inventory and particle size drift
H7 low bed height reducing thermal inertia and heat-absorbing surface contact
cases.discriminating_evidence: Ash recirculation feeder found in the tripped state (no annunciation) together with falling bed differential pressure. Fuel CV and low PA explain a general upward drift; loss of recirculated cool ash removes the specific mechanism the design relies on to hold bed temperature down and explains why the rise ran away. Go observe (not in the six tags): ash recirculation feeder run status and a dedicated alarm; bed differential pressure / bed height on each compartment; compartment-wise PA flow distribution and O2 at economiser outlet (here falling); coal CV / ash / ash-fusion temperature on the consignment vs the feeder calibration; multiple thermocouples on the affected compartment cross-checked against neighbours.
cases.root_cause: Bed temperature runaway to the sintering range from loss of the ash recirculation cooling and bed-inventory path, combined with an uncompensated increase in fuel calorific value and a partially choked PA line reducing fluidising air on the affected compartments. Systemic: no proceduralised combustion re-setting for fuel property changes (no ash-fusion testing on receipt), and the safety-relevant ash recirculation system neither alarmed nor monitored.

cases.title: Furnace draught high / furnace explosion - deflagration after a defeated purge
hypotheses: H1 furnace explosion from ignition of accumulated un-burnt fuel after an inadequate purge
H2 faulty ID / FD / PA / SA fan control causing a pressurisation transient
H3 un-controlled fuel entry through a leaking oil shut-off valve or excessive coal feeding
H4 disturbed / secondary combustion in the back-pass
H5 sudden loss of ID fan or ID damper control pressurising the furnace
H6 faulty furnace pressure transmitter
cases.discriminating_evidence: Not observable in the six process tags - the entire signature is on the furnace-pressure trace and the DCS event log. Go observe: shape of the furnace pressure record (a near-instantaneous STEP spike that lifts relief devices identifies a deflagration; a fan/damper fault gives a ramp over seconds to tens of seconds); purge-permissive over-ride entry in the DCS event log with a purge duration far shorter than the required ~5 min at 40% air; explosion-door / relief-panel lift and ducting expansion-joint deformation (physical confirmation the over-pressure was real); post-event flue gas CO indicating an earlier un-burnt fuel accumulation; oil-soaked deposits on the furnace floor; ID/FD fan status (here in auto, normal current).
cases.root_cause: Deflagration on re-ignition of an accumulated un-burnt fuel-air mixture, made possible by a passing oil-burner shut-off valve and by omission of the mandatory purge. Systemic: a safety-critical interlock (purge permissive) could be defeated by a single operator without authorisation or review, within a management system that tolerated known passing fuel valves and repeated flame failures as routine.

cases.title: Flame failure on the light-up oil burner - degraded atomisation plus detector fouling
hypotheses: H1 poor fuel quality - dirty oil, water contamination, wrong viscosity
H2 improper atomisation - choked tip, low atomising steam pressure, worn nozzle
H3 faulty flame scanner / photocell giving a false loss-of-flame signal
H4 failure of the combustion air blower or insufficient combustion air
H5 high furnace pressure disturbing the flame front
H6 ignition system fault - spark plug gap, HT transformer, ignition timing
cases.discriminating_evidence: Occurs only during light-up / very low bed temperature - not observable in the six running-plant tags. Go observe: a repeatable (not random) loss of flame 30-60 s after establishment on successive attempts (genuine combustion failure) vs a visually-confirmed flame with a weak scanner signal (a detection failure - fouled photocell); LDO day-tank sample for free water and sediment; burner tip nozzle holes for choking; atomising steam / air pressure vs the burner OEM requirement; spark plug condition and electrode gap; combustion-air blower discharge pressure; furnace draught held in band (here -5 to -15 mmwc throughout, ruling out H5).
cases.root_cause: Loss of a stable light-up flame from degraded atomisation - water and sediment in the LDO choked the burner nozzle, with low atomising steam pressure and marginal combustion air, so the flame could not sustain itself; a separately developing photocell fouling added a false loss-of-flame indication. Systemic: the whole light-up system is standby equipment maintained reactively, so multiple hidden failures accumulated and appeared together on demand.

cases.title: Water wall / screen / evaporator tube failure - fireside erosion to rupture
hypotheses: H1 starvation / overheating from low drum level causing DNB and short-term overheat failure
H2 fireside erosion of the tube by bed material at the bed-to-freeboard transition, thinning to burst
H3 waterside deposits causing local overheating and pitting
H4 circulation impaired by an open low-point drain starving the affected circuit
H5 original manufacturing / weld defect
H6 corrosion - caustic gouging or hydrogen damage from poor water chemistry
cases.discriminating_evidence: Rising feed-water-to-steam ratio (feed 2-3 t/h over steam) WITH boiler-water conductivity FALLING - the circuit is being diluted, which establishes a pressure-part leak and excludes every non-leak explanation of the water imbalance. Go observe (not in the six tags): boiler-water conductivity trend (falling = leak; rising = concentration / feed-control fault; a large CBD loss would also lower it); make-up water consumption rate; furnace listening check for a hissing steam leak; furnace draught stability (here fluctuating); local vs sharp bed temperature drop near the leak; whether drum level can still be held on one BFP. At inspection the fracture morphology (thin-lipped longitudinal split at a broadly thinned zone) confirms erosion over overheating or corrosion.
cases.root_cause: Fireside erosion of a water wall tube by circulating bed material in the high-velocity bed-to-freeboard transition zone, progressively thinning the wall until it split longitudinally; internal deposits contributed by raising local metal temperature. Systemic: a foreseeable wear-out mechanism with no thickness-monitoring task, wear shields removed without engineering review, and an uncontrolled operating envelope (excess air, bed height, ash abrasiveness).

cases.title: APH-PA / APH-SA tube failure - cold-end acid dew point corrosion
hypotheses: H1 cold-end corrosion from operating below the acid dew point (fuel sulphur plus low metal temperature)
H2 erosion of tubes by ash at the tube inlets
H3 mechanical failure - thermal fatigue at tube-to-tube-sheet joints, differential expansion
H4 faulty O2 / gas temperature instrumentation giving a spurious leakage signature
H5 air leakage elsewhere in the duct or casing rather than through the APH tubes
H6 fouling / plugging of the APH rather than leakage
cases.discriminating_evidence: Not visible in the six process tags except a slow bed-temperature drift over WEEKS (less effective primary air reaches the bed). Go observe: ESP inlet O2 RISING with no change in the combustion-air setting AND APH outlet flue gas temperature FALLING (the defining air-to-gas leakage pair); PA and SA fan motor current higher for the same delivered wind-box air flow (confirms an air-to-gas leak, not a duct-to-atmosphere leak); gas-side differential pressure across the APH NOT rising (rules out fouling); cold-end metal temperature vs the calculated acid dew point for the actual fuel sulphur; damage concentrated in the coldest rows with acidic corrosion products (vs erosion at the gas-entry face, vs fatigue at the tube sheets).
cases.root_cause: Sulphuric acid condensation on cold-end APH tube surfaces running below the acid dew point, causing progressive external wall loss and perforation, with ash erosion at the tube inlets as a secondary contributor. Systemic: no cold-end metal temperature control or monitoring, no acid-dew-point recalculation after a fuel sulphur increase, and no periodic APH leakage measurement.

cases.title: Loss of coal feeders from a common electrical cause - MCC incomer single-phasing
hypotheses: H1 common electrical supply failure to all feeder drives (MCC / incomer / bus fault)
H2 process interlock trip - bed temperature, furnace pressure, drum level, MS temperature high
H3 PA fan trip causing the feeder trip interlock to act
H4 VFD fault common to the drives - shared control supply or common firmware fault
H5 mechanical jamming of all feeders (implausible, formally considered)
H6 operator error - all feeders stopped from DCS
cases.discriminating_evidence: All six feeder drives reporting an incoming supply abnormality (phase loss / under-voltage) at the same instant. Simultaneity across six independent mechanical drives is near-conclusive for a supply-side common cause, and the VFD fault-code content separates it from a process interlock, an operator stop and a drive-internal fault. Go observe (not in the six tags): the six VFD fault codes and their timestamps; the MCC incomer protection operation in the electrical event log; absence of any preceding bed temperature / drum level / furnace pressure excursion (process interlocks leave a clear trend trace); PA fan status (here running normally); DCS operator command logs (no stop command). Distinguish from a fuel hang-up (Case 6) by the step-vs-ramp onset and by all compartments falling equally rather than compartment-selectively.
cases.root_cause: Total loss of fuel input from a degraded connection on one phase of the MCC incomer producing single-phasing, tripping all six coal feeder VFDs on phase loss. Systemic: all six feeders on one un-segregated bus section (a single-point-of-failure), and an electrical PM programme with no thermography and no connection-torque verification.

cases.title: Hot bed material leakage / back-fire in a PA line - throttled branch damper after maintenance
hypotheses: H1 low or interrupted PA flow in one branch letting hot bed material back-flow into the line
H2 PA fan trip or header pressure loss
H3 distributor nozzle failure / missing caps letting bed material into the wind box
H4 excessive bed height increasing static head against the air supply
H5 bed ash drain valve leaking or left open, drawing material into the line
H6 coal feeding to a poorly fluidised compartment causing local sintering and defluidisation
cases.discriminating_evidence: Confined to one compartment - the six-tag averages barely move. Go observe: PA flow to the affected compartment LOW while the PA header pressure stays NORMAL (isolates the restriction to that branch and excludes a fan/header cause); glowing hot material and rising surface temperature on the vertical portion of that PA line; erratic, non-uniform bed temperature in that one compartment only; bed differential pressure normal on all compartments (rules out excessive bed height); the bed ash drain valve verified closed and cold; the maintenance record showing recent work on that line with no damper restoration check.
cases.root_cause: Insufficient primary air velocity in one branch line after a PA damper was left throttled following maintenance, so the line dynamic pressure could no longer oppose the fluidised-bed static head and hot particles back-flowed and accumulated in the vertical portion. Systemic: no post-maintenance restoration checklist for damper positions, no compartment-wise PA flow measurement, and no PA line temperature monitoring.

cases.title: Boiler feed pump failure - cavitation from NPSH loss on low deaerator level
hypotheses: H1 loss of NPSH from a low deaerator level causing cavitation
H2 choked suction strainer restricting flow
H3 mechanical failure of bearings or rotor - misalignment or unbalance
H4 minimum recirculation valve failing to open, causing low-flow operation and overheating
H5 electrical fault - motor protection relay operation, low bearing oil pressure
H6 discharge-side restriction increasing pump load
H7 deaerator water temperature too high for the available static head (flashing at suction)
cases.discriminating_evidence: The standby pump replicating the same behaviour within seconds of starting - a defect internal to one pump cannot transfer to another, so identical behaviour in two independent machines points to the shared suction condition. Go observe (not in the six tags): deaerator level falling below its low alarm AHEAD of every pump symptom (the earliest indication); BFP suction pressure and NPSH margin; audible cavitation / crackling at the pump; vibration rising to the >9.3 mm/s trip; pump bearing temperature >110 degC and mechanical seal leakage (these follow the vibration, so they are consequences); differential pressure across the suction strainer (a contributor); discharge header pressure FALLING (rules out a discharge restriction).
cases.root_cause: Cavitation of the boiler feed pump from loss of net positive suction head - a condensate transfer failure let the deaerator level fall below the NPSH required, with a partially choked suction strainer removing the remaining margin; the standby pump cavitated on start for the same reason. Systemic: the deaerator level is a single-point common-cause vulnerability for both feed pump trains, protected only by an alarm and not by an interlock or a reliable condensate transfer system.

cases.title: Loss of PA fan with bed defluidisation - motor cooling fouling plus hidden standby failure
hypotheses: H1 PA fan motor thermal failure from blocked cooling air passages
H2 motor electrical fault - winding insulation failure, earth fault, protection relay operation
H3 fan overload from high PA outlet pressure (choked PA lines / closed dampers)
H4 motor bearing failure causing heating
H5 MCC fault or loss of supply
H6 consequential trip from another interlock - drum level, furnace pressure, ID or SA fan trip
H7 failure of the standby PA fan auto-start (a separate, second failure)
cases.discriminating_evidence: Divergence between motor WINDING temperature (rising over ~30 min) and motor CURRENT (normal): an overload would raise current with temperature, an electrical fault would trip protection first, so a winding-temperature rise alone identifies loss of the cooling air path. Go observe (not in the six tags): PA fan motor winding temperature vs motor current trend; standby PA fan auto-start command present with no run feed-back (the hidden second failure); PA header pressure collapse and loss of primary air; all coal feeders tripping simultaneously on the designed PA-fan-trip interlock; erratic bed temperature indication and low furnace draught after fluidising air is lost. On the six averaged tags this looks the same as a total feeder loss (Case 14).
cases.root_cause: Two independent failures in sequence: PA fan motor winding overheating from coal-dust fouling of the cooling air passages tripped the running fan, and a defective run feed-back contact aborted the standby PA fan auto-start. The combination removed all fluidising air, the bed defluidised, the feeders tripped on interlock and hot bed material migrated into the PA lines. Systemic: no scheduled motor cleaning for the known dusty environment and no periodic proof test of standby auto-start.
